recap_lines: A material is values per pixel, and lighting turns them into colour.
Roughness runs from mirror to dull, and smoothness runs the other way.
Only the base colour is decoded from sRGB, the other maps are data.
A normal map fakes bumps, and Godot expects green pointing up.
An ORM map packs occlusion, roughness and metallic into red, green and blue.
Texel density, not resolution, decides how sharp a texture looks on a surface.
bookends.command: Quiz me on material and texture terms with short game-making cases, one at a time. Hold back the answer until I reply, then tell me if I was right.

beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. Newcomers often think every texture is a picture. Only the base colour is. A normal map, a roughness map and a packed ORM map are numbers stored in an image, and decoding them as colour corrupts them. Materials are full of look-alikes like that. This film goes through the terms group by group, each one shown, so you can name the exact one.

beats.narration_text: Now the same material under three lights. PBR, physically based rendering, stores a few measured quantities per pixel, so a material holds up under any light. The albedo, metallic and roughness never change here, yet the ringed point comes out three different colours, because only the light moved. For example, a wooden crate with a PBR material looks right in a sunny courtyard and in a torch-lit cellar, with no second set of textures for each.

beats.narration_text: A flat normal texel, one hundred twenty-eight, one hundred twenty-eight, two hundred fifty-five, read two ways. Read as linear data, its value is zero point five zero two, and it points straight out. Decoded as sRGB by mistake, it drops to zero point two one six, the surface tilts thirty-eight point eight degrees, and the lighting is twenty-two percent too dark. For example, if an agent marks a brick wall's normal map as colour, the whole wall shades lopsided, though the file itself is fine.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap. A material is values per pixel, and lighting turns them into colour. Roughness runs from mirror to dull, and smoothness runs the other way. Only the base colour is decoded from sRGB, the other maps are data. A normal map fakes bumps, and Godot expects green pointing up. An ORM map packs occlusion, roughness and metallic into red, green and blue. Texel density, not resolution, decides how sharp a texture looks on a surface.
